Sample Size for a Targeted Regression Coefficient

Source: R/ss_power_reg_coef.R
ss_power_reg_coef.Rd

Determine the necessary sample size for a targeted regression coefficient or determine the degree of power given a specified sample size

Usage

ss_power_reg_coef(
  true_R2_Y_X = NULL,
  true_R2_Y_X_without_j = NULL,
  p = NULL,
  desired_power = 0.85,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  directional = FALSE,
  true_reg_coef_j = NULL,
  true_sd_X = NULL,
  true_sd_Y = NULL,
  true_R2_j_X_without_j = NULL,
  true_cor_XX = NULL,
  true_cor_YX = NULL,
  which_predictor = NULL,
  true_f2 = NULL,
  specified_N = NULL,
  print_iter = FALSE
)

Arguments

true_R2_Y_X

Population squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting the dependent variable (i.e., Y) from the p predictor variables (i.e., the X variables)

true_R2_Y_X_without_j

Population squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting the dependent variable (i.e., Y) from the p-1 predictor variables, where the one not used is the predictor of interest

p

Number of predictor variables in the full model, a single whole number of at least 1. It is required when the effect is given through true_R2_Y_X, true_reg_coef_j, or true_f2, and is not given with true_cor_XX and true_cor_YX, whose dimension sets it

desired_power

Desired degree of statistical power for the test of targeted regression coefficient

alpha_level

Type I error rate

directional

Whether or not a direction or a nondirectional test is to be used (usually directional=FALSE)

true_reg_coef_j

Population value of the regression coefficient for the predictor of interest, the name it has in ss_aipe_reg_coef and ss_aipe_rc. It is on the scale that true_sd_X and true_sd_Y describe: with both standard deviations 1 it is the standardized coefficient

true_sd_X

Population standard deviation for the predictor variable of interest

true_sd_Y

Population standard deviation for the outcome variable

true_R2_j_X_without_j

Population squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting the predictor variable of interest from the remaining p-1 predictor variables

true_cor_XX

Population correlation matrix for the p predictor variables: symmetric, with 1 on the diagonal, and positive definite; another matrix is refused with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid

true_cor_YX

Population vector of correlation coefficient between the p predictor variables and the criterion variable; with true_cor_XX it must imply a squared multiple correlation below 1 (the correlation matrix of the outcome and the predictors is then positive definite)

which_predictor

Identifies the predictor of interest when true_cor_XX and true_cor_YX are specified: a single whole number from 1 to p, its position in true_cor_XX

true_f2

Cohen's (1988) definition for an effect size for a targeted regression coefficient: (true_R2_Y_X-true_R2_Y_X_without_j)/(1-true_R2_Y_X)

specified_N

Sample size for which power should be evaluated. This is the total sample size.

print_iter

If the progress of the iterative procedure is printed to the screen as the iterations are occurring

Value

ss

Either the necessary sample size or the specified sample size, depending if one is interested in determining the necessary sample size given a desired degree of statistical power or if one is interested in the determining the value of statistical power given a specified sample size, respectively

actual_power

Actual power of the situation described

noncentral_t_parm

Value of the noncentral distribution for the appropriate t-distribution

true_f

Cohen's f at the planning values, the effect size for the noncentral t-distribution; this is the square root of true_f2, because true_f2 is the effect size using an F-distribution. When the effect is given through true_reg_coef_j it carries the sign of the coefficient.

Details

Determines the necessary sample size given a desired level of statistical power. Alternatively, determines the statistical power for a given a specified sample size. There are a number of ways that the specification regarding the size of the regression coefficient can be entered. The most basic, and often the simplest, is to specify true_R2_Y_X and true_R2_Y_X_without_j. See the examples section for several options.

Power is computed from a noncentral t distribution with noncentrality \(\sqrt{N}\,f\), which treats the predictors as fixed (their values held constant across hypothetical replications). This is the standard fixed-predictor power analysis; under random predictors, where the predictor values themselves vary from sample to sample, the sample size required for a given level of power is somewhat larger. The test is the case of ss_power_R2_change with one predictor added and fixed predictors (true_R2_Y_X is its true_R2_full and true_R2_Y_X_without_j its true_R2_restricted); that function also plans the test with random predictors and the test of a set of added predictors.

With true_cor_XX and true_cor_YX, the squared multiple correlation of the full model is \(\rho_{YX}' \mathbf{R}_{XX}^{-1} \rho_{YX}\), where \(\rho_{YX}\) is true_cor_YX and \(\mathbf{R}_{XX}\) is true_cor_XX, and that of the model without the predictor of interest is the same quantity with the predictor's row and column removed from \(\mathbf{R}_{XX}\) and its element from \(\rho_{YX}\). With a single predictor (p of 1) the model without it has no predictors and its squared multiple correlation is 0, so the effect is that of true_f2 \(= \rho^2 / (1 - \rho^2)\), where \(\rho\) is true_cor_YX.

When the planning values give the predictor an effect of exactly 0 (true_f2 of 0, equal squared multiple correlations, or a true_reg_coef_j of 0), the null hypothesis is true and the t statistic has the central t distribution at every sample size, so the probability that the test rejects is alpha_level, for the two-sided test and for the directional one alike. A sample size is then defined only for a desired_power no greater than alpha_level, and it is the smallest admissible one, p + 2; a larger desired_power is refused at once with a condition of class dmar_effect_zero. With specified_N the power at that size is returned, which is alpha_level. For an effect that is not 0 the power rises with the sample size, and a desired_power that no sample size up to 10,000,000 attains is refused at once with a condition of class dmar_computation_failed.

References

Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2008). Sample size planning with applications to multiple regression: Power and accuracy for omnibus and targeted effects. In P. Alasuutari, L. Bickman, & J. Brannen (Eds.), The Sage handbook of social research methods (pp. 166–192). Sage.

Maxwell, S. E. (2000). Sample size and multiple regression analysis. Psychological Methods, 5(4), 434–458. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.5.4.434

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 4 on individual comparisons of means and Chapter 6 on trend analysis.)

Maxwell, S. E., Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2008). Sample size planning for statistical power and accuracy in parameter estimation. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 537–563. doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093735

Anderson, S. F., Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2017). Sample-size planning for more accurate statistical power: A method adjusting sample effect sizes for publication bias and uncertainty. Psychological Science, 28(11), 1547–1562. doi:10.1177/0956797617723724

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

Cor.Mat <- rbind(
  c(1.00, 0.53, 0.58, 0.60, 0.46, 0.66),
  c(0.53, 1.00, 0.35, 0.07, 0.14, 0.43),
  c(0.58, 0.35, 1.00, 0.18, 0.29, 0.50),
  c(0.60, 0.07, 0.18, 1.00, 0.30, 0.26),
  c(0.46, 0.14, 0.29, 0.30, 1.00, 0.30),
  c(0.66, 0.43, 0.50, 0.26, 0.30, 1.00)
)

true_cor_XX <- Cor.Mat[2:6, 2:6]
true_cor_YX <- Cor.Mat[1, 2:6]

# Method 1
ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = 0.7826786, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = 0.7363697, p = 5,
                  alpha_level = .05, directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       40   
#>  actual_power      0.810
#>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920
#>  true_f            0.462

# Method 2
ss_power_reg_coef(alpha_level = .05, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,
                  which_predictor = 5,
                  directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       40   
#>  actual_power      0.810
#>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920
#>  true_f            0.462

# Method 3
# Here, true_reg_coef_j is the standardized regression coefficient. Had true_reg_coef_j
# been the unstandardized regression coefficient, true_sd_X and true_sd_Y
# would have been the standard deviation for the X variable of
# interest and Y, respectively.
ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = 0.7826786, true_R2_j_X_without_j = 0.3652136,
                  true_reg_coef_j = 0.2700964,
                  p = 5, alpha_level = .05, true_sd_X = 1, true_sd_Y = 1, directional = FALSE,
                  desired_power = .80)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       40   
#>  actual_power      0.810
#>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920
#>  true_f            0.462

# Method 4
ss_power_reg_coef(alpha_level = .05, true_f2 = 0.2130898, p = 5,
                  directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       40   
#>  actual_power      0.810
#>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920
#>  true_f            0.462

# Power given a specified N and squared multiple correlation coefficients.
ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = 0.7826786, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = 0.7363697, specified_N = 25,
                  p = 5, alpha_level = .05, directional = FALSE)
#>  term              value
#>  specified_N       25   
#>  actual_power      0.591
#>  noncentral_t_parm 2.308
#>  true_f            0.462

# Power given a specified N and effect size.
ss_power_reg_coef(alpha_level = .05, true_f2 = 0.2130898, p = 5, specified_N = 25,
                  directional = FALSE)
#>  term              value
#>  specified_N       25   
#>  actual_power      0.591
#>  noncentral_t_parm 2.308
#>  true_f            0.462

# Reproducing Maxwell's (2000, p. 445) Example
Cor.Mat.Maxwell <- rbind(
  c(1.00, 0.35, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20),
  c(0.35, 1.00, 0.40, 0.40, 0.40, 0.40),
  c(0.20, 0.40, 1.00, 0.45, 0.45, 0.45),
  c(0.20, 0.40, 0.45, 1.00, 0.45, 0.45),
  c(0.20, 0.40, 0.45, 0.45, 1.00, 0.45),
  c(0.20, 0.40, 0.45, 0.45, 0.45, 1.00)
)

RHO.XX.Maxwell <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[2:6, 2:6]
Rho.YX.Maxwell <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[1, 2:6]
R2.Maxwell <- Rho.YX.Maxwell %*% solve(RHO.XX.Maxwell) %*% Rho.YX.Maxwell

RHO.XX.Maxwell.no.1 <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[3:6, 3:6]
Rho.YX.Maxwell.no.1 <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[1, 3:6]
R2.Maxwell.no.1 <-
  Rho.YX.Maxwell.no.1 %*% solve(RHO.XX.Maxwell.no.1) %*% Rho.YX.Maxwell.no.1

# This procedure arrives at N = 111, whereas Maxwell (2000, p. 445)
# reports N = 113. The two differ because of the noncentrality
# parameterization, not rounding: this function uses the fixed-predictor
# noncentrality sqrt(N) * f (see Details), while the tabled value rests on
# Cohen's (1988) convention. Neither is a random-predictor result; under
# random predictors, where the predictor values vary across replications,
# the sample size needed for the same power is larger still.
ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = R2.Maxwell, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = R2.Maxwell.no.1, p = 5,
                  alpha_level = .05, directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       111  
#>  actual_power      0.801
#>  noncentral_t_parm 2.833
#>  true_f            0.269
